appraisal_events.evidence: Her amiability is traced to a catechism of 'préceptes orgueilleusement humbles d'un snobisme évangélique' instilled by her mother ('sois bonne pour les petits... mais bien entendu jamais d'invitations à tes soirées'), and her constant show of not feeling superior is likened to the instinctive deference of old family servants.
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator exposes the princess's celebrated humility as a rehearsed, class-inherited performance rather than a personal virtue, deepening the earlier deflation of her figure.

appraisal_events.evidence: Unable to place the unknown guest, Bréauté assumes he must have 'des titres tout à fait extraordinaires' to be present, and once the unfamiliar name is given he is certain the narrator is 'quelque célébrité,' multiplying bows, knowing looks, and monocle-filtered smiles.
appraisal_events.explanation: A seasoned society figure showers the narrator with exaggerated deference, mistaking his mere presence in the duchess's exclusive salon for proof of extraordinary distinction.

appraisal_events.evidence: Her salon's power to consecrate is proven by fact: she dared invite the painter Detaille to the reception for the King and Queen of England, and had Mlle Reichenberg recite verses before the king, 'un fait sans précédent dans les annales des raouts,' leaving the whole Faubourg Saint-Germain enviously impressed.
appraisal_events.explanation: Concrete instances establish the duchesse's salon as an unmatched instrument of social consecration, elevating her local prestige as a hostess.

appraisal_events.evidence: Imagined as luminously Sicilian, sovereign of an antique rose-cubed city, the prince turns out to be 'le vulgaire hanneton' who pirouettes with a heavy, self-satisfied bow, as independent of his name as of an artwork he owns without ever having looked at it — 'il ne restait plus un atome de charme à retirer' from him.
appraisal_events.explanation: The prince's actual person is shown to be utterly devoid of anything princely, comically emptied of the poetic aura his name evokes.

status_effects.explanation: Her humility is unmasked as an inherited class performance rather than personal virtue, continuing to deflate the romantic image around her.
Bréauté's visible, repeated deference publicly treats him as a possible celebrity, a witnessed mark of momentary standing within the salon.
Cited precedents of her salon's daring, successful inclusions raise her local reputation as a uniquely powerful hostess.
He is thoroughly deflated on encounter, shown void of any of the princely charm his name had promised.

ambiguities: M. de Guermantes's seemingly sincere praise of the princesse de Parme as 'une très bonne femme' who excels at being a grande dame sits alongside the narrator's more ironizing account of her rehearsed humility; the passage does not fully resolve whether the duke's admiration is itself ironized or genuine.
